name: End-of-the-day betting effect
aliases: End of the day betting effect
statement: Betting moves towards longshots in the last race of the day, a shift reproduced in laboratory gambles and not significant in the largest set of racetrack data.
meaning: The claim is about a change within a session, not about the level of the longshot bias. Racetrack odds already price longshots badly on every race, which is the favourite-longshot bias, entry 220 here. This effect says the pricing gets worse in the final race, because the money moves further away from the favourite once bettors know no race follows. Field studies measure it by comparing odds or rates of return in the last race with the same quantities earlier in the card, so the object is again a pool price rather than an observed person. The standard explanation is a mental account opened at the start of the day and closed at the end. Most bettors are losing by the last race, because the track keeps a share of every pool, and a longshot is the only bet large enough to clear the day's deficit. That account makes a testable prediction: the shift should come from bettors who are behind. Laboratory work has now tested it. The prediction failed in two experiments and was only marginal in the third.

origin.note: "Stability of Choices among Uncertain Alternatives" analysed 9,605 races run at several American tracks between 1947 and 1953, and found longshot betting rising in the eighth race alone rather than across the card. McGlothlin wrote that horses with a high probability of winning and low payoffs "become even more unpopular in the last race". The paper was not obtainable on 21 September 2026. JSTOR answered with a script challenge rather than a paywall, and the World Scientific volume that reprints it answered with a Cloudflare interstitial. Its sample, its dates and that sentence are taken from McKenzie and colleagues, who quote it from page 611 of the published article.

evidence: Four further field studies are named in the literature, and all of them are described here as McKenzie and colleagues describe them, because none was readable during this check. Ali compared the last race with the first two across 20,247 harness races at three New York tracks between 1970 and 1974. Asch, Malkiel and Quandt took the 1978 thoroughbred season at one New Jersey track, 729 races, and found a larger longshot bias in the last two races combined than across all races. Metzger is described by them as examining 11,313 American races run in 1978, with more longshot betting in the last race and an anomalous result for the first. Her own abstract at Crossref gives the sample as 12,316 races and calls the finding an increasing risk preference within the day. Her paper could not be read here, so the two accounts are left standing apart. Kopelman and Minkin used 286 races at a New York track in 1986 and found posted odds less favourable for favourites in the last race. Add McGlothlin's 9,605 races and McKenzie and colleagues put the five samples at more than 42,000 races. None of them can say whether a given bettor was ahead or behind. McKenzie and five co-authors built the missing measurement in the laboratory. Their first experiment gave 140 undergraduates eight rounds of a choice between two gambles. The favourite paid one point half the time, the longshot nine points a tenth of the time, and each lost one point otherwise. Both had an expected value of zero. Longshot choices were 19 percentage points higher in the last round than in the others, with a standard error of 0.04 across 1,120 choices. Adding a linear trend left a last-round effect of 11 points on top of it. The share of participants in the loss domain fell across rounds, from 66 percent before round two to 55 percent before round eight, while longshot betting rose.

replication.headline: Three laboratory experiments produce the last-round shift reliably, and the largest racetrack sample ever assembled shows no significant version of it.
replication.detail: Snowberg and Wolfers hold official Jockey Club records of 6,403,712 horse starts run in the United States from 1992 to 2001. The rate-of-return curve in their figure 1 covers 5,610,580 starts, with a dashed line separating the last race of each card. They write that the point estimates differ slightly and that the differences are not statistically significant, and conclude that whatever earlier data showed is no longer evident. Both figures count starts rather than races, and the same file holds 865,934 races. Entry 220 here records the same null. The laboratory record runs the other way. McKenzie and colleagues manipulated which round was the last one, so position could be read as a cause rather than inferred from a single card. In their second experiment, 254 undergraduates played either eight rounds or ten, and were told only just before the final round which it was. Round eight drew 69 percent longshot choices when it was last and 56 percent when it was the eighth of ten, chi-square 4.44 with one degree of freedom, p = .035. The third experiment paid 224 undergraduates in cash and used real horse names and posted odds from a New York track in 2004. Race eight drew 65 percent longshot choices when last against 50 percent when eighth of ten, chi-square 5.24, p = .022. Mean earnings were $1.98. The loss-recouping account failed all three times. In experiment one those in the gain domain showed the larger last-round shift. In experiment two the interaction the account predicts was absent, chi-square below one, p = .43, and in experiment three it was marginal at p = .10. Later work has kept the effect and narrowed it sharply. Wang, Zhang and Xing gave 104 participants twenty rounds with a safe option and two risky ones, a coin paying double and a die paying six times the stake. Half were told at the outset that the task ran to twenty rounds and half were not. The last-round rise in high-risk investment appeared only among those who had been told. Among those who had not, the safe option rose at the end instead, by 0.14 on the authors' ending effect score of investment likelihood, and the high-risk option did not move at all. Their replication therefore holds only where the ending is known in advance, which is a condition the racetrack studies assume rather than test. Wang, Yin and Xing used a large online football gambling dataset and report that bettors took more risk at the end while preferring the lower-risk options, which they call a bounded ending effect. Dou and Ye, using a guessing game, observed the ending effect only in the gain group of their first experiment.

study.cite: McKenzie, C. R. M., Sher, S., Müller-Trede, J., Lin, C., Liersch, M. J., & Rawstron, A. G. (2016). Are longshots only for losers? A new look at the last race effect. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 29(1), 25-36.

limits: The five historical field studies were not read, and each was refused for a different reason on 21 September 2026. JSTOR served McGlothlin as a script challenge. The University of Chicago Press refused Ali with a 403 and Elsevier refused Asch and colleagues with a 403. Sage refused Metzger and Kopelman and Minkin, answering a plain and a browser user agent alike with a 403. The World Scientific volume reprinting two of them answered with a Cloudflare interstitial. OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar record all five as closed with no repository copy, and searches of Crossref, PubMed, the open web and the authors' pages found none. Every figure attributed to them above comes from McKenzie and colleagues' description, except Metzger's sample, where her own Crossref abstract disagrees and both numbers are given. No field test of the effect on racetrack data more recent than Snowberg and Wolfers' 2001 cut-off was found in those same venues on that date. The modern evidence is laboratory work plus one online football dataset. The laboratory experiments use undergraduates, gambles with an expected value of zero, and stakes that paid a mean of $1.98. A racetrack takes about 18 percent of each pool and the sums are real, so the two settings differ in the direction that matters most for a loss-recouping story. McKenzie and colleagues say so themselves, noting that only their paid experiment produced any evidence for that account. Their own explanation, that people like to end a sequence with the most exciting event, was not tested against an alternative in these experiments.
misreadings: The commonest error is the one the name carries. Wikipedia's article defines the effect as bettors taking higher risks at the end of a session "to try to make up for losses", and its worked example has the bettor who is up $200 choosing a safe bet and the one who is down $320 choosing 35 to 1. McKenzie and colleagues tested exactly that split three times and found the last-round shift in both domains, larger among winners in the first experiment. A second error is treating the effect as a stronger dose of the favourite-longshot bias. The two are separable, and Snowberg and Wolfers' data separate them: the longshot bias is there in millions of starts and the last-race change is not. A third is the claim, repeated in the same Wikipedia article, that the shift is large enough to make a show bet on the last race's favourite profitable despite the track's cut. Snowberg and Wolfers report that positive returns to extreme favourites appear in none of their datasets. A fourth is reading the laboratory replications as confirmation of the field claim. They show that people take more risk in a round labelled the last one, which is a finding about sequences. Wang, Zhang and Xing make the point sharper: unlabelled, the last round drew no extra risk at all. The racetrack version of the effect has not been recovered from recent prices.
